### Problem: Maximum Frequency Stack {#sec-ds-p3-freqstack}

::: {.p-statement}
Design a `FreqStack` with two operations:

- `push(val)` — push an integer onto the stack;
- `pop()` — remove and return the most frequent element; if several are tied, return the one **closest to the top** (pushed most recently).

$0 \le$ `val` $\le 10^9$, at most $2\cdot10^4$ calls in total, and `pop` is never called on an empty stack. Pushing `5, 7, 5, 7, 4, 5` gives frequencies $5{:}3,\ 7{:}2,\ 4{:}1$, and four pops return `5, 7, 5, 4`: first the only value with frequency $3$, then `7` beats the remaining `5` (both at frequency $2$) because it was pushed more recently, and so on.

Source: [LC 895 · Maximum Frequency Stack](https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-frequency-stack/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Make the frequency an index: `levels[f]` is a stack of the values at the moment they *reached* frequency $f$. A value joins `levels[f]` exactly when its count becomes $f$, so the top of the highest non-empty level is the most frequent value and, among those, the newest. One integer `maxf` (the highest non-empty level) makes `pop` a single stack pop (@sec-ds-a3).
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Rescan on pop.** Keep one list; on `pop`, count every value and take the maximum by `(frequency, newest index)`. $O(n)$ per pop. This class is the naive model.
2. **Frequency levels.** `count[x]` per value, `levels[f]` = stack of values that reached $f$, and a cursor `maxf`. Push bumps a count and lands on the new level; pop drains the top level and lowers `maxf` when it empties. $O(1)$ both.
3. **Levels in an array.** Frequencies are $1, 2, \ldots, \text{maxf}$ with no gaps (a value at frequency $f$ also sits on every lower level), so `levels` can be a list of stacks whose length *is* `maxf`. A push that reaches a new frequency appends a stack; a pop that empties the top stack removes it.

**Operation contract (final form).** Invariant **I**: `levels[f-1]` (0-based) holds, bottom to top in push order, every value $x$ with `count[x]` $\ge f$, once each; all stacks are non-empty; so `len(levels)` is the maximum frequency.

| Operation | What it does | How **I** survives | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| `push(x)` | `count[x] += 1`; if `count[x] > len(levels)` append an empty stack; push `x` onto stack `count[x]` | $x$ now has frequency $f$ and appears on levels $1..f$; the newest copy is on top of level $f$ | $O(1)$ amortised |
| `pop()` | pop `x` from the last stack; `count[x] -= 1`; drop the stack if it emptied | $x$ leaves only its highest level; lower levels still hold it | $O(1)$ amortised |
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Rescan on pop

::: {.form-next}
One list. `pop` recomputes all frequencies and breaks ties by the newest index. $O(n)$ per pop: this is what the levels buy down to $O(1)$, and it is the model the final form is tested against.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("freqstack", "scan")
    assert str(final) == "pops [5, 7, 5, 4]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
from collections import Counter


class FreqScan:
    def __init__(self):
        self.a = []

    def push(self, x):
        self.a.append(x)

    def pop(self):
        cnt = Counter(self.a)
        newest = {}
        for i, x in enumerate(self.a):
            newest[x] = i                       # last (topmost) index of each value
        best = max(cnt, key=lambda v: (cnt[v], newest[v]))
        del self.a[newest[best]]
        return best


f = FreqScan()
for x in [5, 7, 5, 7, 4, 5]:
    f.push(x)
assert [f.pop() for _ in range(4)] == [5, 7, 5, 4]
```

##### C++

```cpp
class FreqScan {
    vector<int> a;
 public:
    void push(int x) { a.push_back(x); }
    int pop() {
        unordered_map<int, int> cnt, newest;
        for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); ++i) { cnt[a[i]]++; newest[a[i]] = i; }
        int best = a.back();
        for (const auto& kv : cnt) {
            int v = kv.first, c = kv.second, bc = cnt[best];
            if (c > bc || (c == bc && newest[v] > newest[best])) best = v;
        }
        a.erase(a.begin() + newest[best]);
        return best;
    }
};
```
:::

#### Frequency levels

::: {.form-next}
Two dictionaries and a cursor. `count[x]` is a value's frequency; `levels[f]` is a stack of the values that have reached frequency $f$; `maxf` is the highest non-empty level. Push moves `x` up one level, pop drains `maxf` and lowers it if the level empties. Both $O(1)$.
:::

##### Python

```{python}
from collections import defaultdict


class FreqStackDict:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = Counter()
        self.levels = defaultdict(list)
        self.maxf = 0

    def push(self, x):
        self.count[x] += 1
        f = self.count[x]
        self.levels[f].append(x)
        self.maxf = max(self.maxf, f)

    def pop(self):
        x = self.levels[self.maxf].pop()
        self.count[x] -= 1
        if not self.levels[self.maxf]:
            self.maxf -= 1
        return x


f = FreqStackDict()
for x in [5, 7, 5, 7, 4, 5]:
    f.push(x)
assert [f.pop() for _ in range(4)] == [5, 7, 5, 4]
```

##### C++

```cpp
class FreqStackDict {
    unordered_map<int, int> count;
    unordered_map<int, vector<int>> levels;
    int maxf = 0;
 public:
    void push(int x) {
        maxf = max(maxf, ++count[x]);
        levels[count[x]].push_back(x);
    }
    int pop() {
        int x = levels[maxf].back(); levels[maxf].pop_back();
        --count[x];
        if (levels[maxf].empty()) --maxf;
        return x;
    }
};
```
:::

#### Levels in an array

::: {.form-next}
Level numbers have no gaps, so the dictionary of levels becomes a list of stacks and the cursor disappears: the top level is `levels[-1]`. A push that reaches a new frequency appends a stack; a pop that empties the top stack removes it. The stress test interleaves pushes and pops at random against the rescanning model and checks invariant **I**.
:::

```{python}

V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
class FreqStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = Counter()
        self.levels = []                   # levels[f-1] = stack of values with count >= f

    def push(self, x):
        self.count[x] += 1
        f = self.count[x]
        if f > len(self.levels):
            self.levels.append([])
        self.levels[f - 1].append(x)

    def pop(self):
        x = self.levels[-1].pop()
        self.count[x] -= 1
        if not self.levels[-1]:
            self.levels.pop()              # the top level emptied: the max frequency drops by one
        return x

    def check(self):
        for f, lev in enumerate(self.levels, 1):
            assert lev and sorted(lev) == sorted(x for x, c in self.count.items() if c >= f)


f = FreqStack()
for x in [5, 7, 5, 7, 4, 5]:
    f.push(x)
assert [f.pop() for _ in range(4)] == [5, 7, 5, 4]    # the board sample
# stress: random interleaved pushes and pops against the rescanning model
for _ in range(300):
    fast, model = FreqStack(), FreqScan()
    for _ in range(40):
        if model.a and random.random() < 0.4:
            assert fast.pop() == model.pop()
        else:
            x = random.randint(0, 4)
            fast.push(x); model.push(x)
        fast.check()
```

##### C++

```cpp
class FreqStack {
    unordered_map<int, int> count;
    vector<vector<int>> levels;            // levels[f-1]: values with count >= f
 public:
    void push(int x) {
        int f = ++count[x];
        if (f > (int)levels.size()) levels.push_back(vector<int>());
        levels[f - 1].push_back(x);
    }
    int pop() {
        int x = levels.back().back(); levels.back().pop_back();
        --count[x];
        if (levels.back().empty()) levels.pop_back();
        return x;
    }
};
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Rescan on pop:** $O(1)$ push, $O(n)$ pop. **Frequency levels:** $O(1)$ expected per push and pop. **Levels in an array:** the same, with one hash map left (`count`) and no cursor. Space is $O(n)$ for both level forms: each pushed copy lives on exactly one level.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- **Emptying a level**: only then does the maximum frequency drop, and by exactly one, because the popped value is still on the level below (exercise 14 proves it).
- **A value pushed again after being popped**: its count was decremented, so the new copy lands on the right level; nothing else needs resetting.
- **Ties across levels cannot happen**: only the top level is read, so recency is decided purely by the push order within that level.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Tracking timestamps explicitly** as a second sort key. The order inside a level already encodes recency.
- **A heap keyed by (frequency, push time)**: push `(count after the push, time, x)` and pop the maximum. It is correct (each entry stands for one pushed copy at the level it reached), but it costs $O(\log n)$ per operation; the levels give the same order in $O(1)$.
- **Lowering `maxf` on every pop** instead of only when the level empties.
:::

**Variants.** @sec-ds-p3-allone is the same counter of counters queried by *key* (`getMinKey`/`getMaxKey`) instead of by pop, so the levels become a doubly linked chain. The LFU cache (LC 460) keeps, inside each frequency level, a recency order with deletions in the middle.

::: {.practice}
- [LC 460 · LFU Cache](https://leetcode.com/problems/lfu-cache/){difficulty="Hard"} — frequency levels whose members are kept in LRU order, with a cursor for the minimum frequency instead of the maximum.
:::
